accuracy.evidence: Matches the England Year 6 grammar appendix item 'layout devices such as headings, sub-headings, columns, bullets or tables to structure text' and CCSS W.4.2a/W.5.2a formatting such as headings. Hedgehog facts were checked: they eat beetles, worms and caterpillars, roam about two kilometres a night, hibernate roughly November to March, need a 13 cm fence gap, and milk upsets them. Grey squirrels do not hibernate.

misconceptions.evidence: Decoys hit the slips teachers report: a vague sub-heading like Interesting facts, a full sentence used as a sub-heading, bullets used for ordered steps, a table without column headers, and turning linked because/so reasoning into bullets. Each wrong drop gives its own message, for example the full-sentence chip explains a sub-heading is a short label.

lab_distinct.evidence: flaglayout is the only lab where learners drag sub-headings onto prose sections, sort content cards into four layout devices, file facts into table cells by reading row and column headers, and swipe tips into Do and Don't columns. It differs from flagtstr text-structure ordering and flagpic picture captions, and the 30 percent shingle gate passed against every flag file.

lab_teaches.evidence: Every step makes the learner use the device, not just name it: they label sections, choose bullets versus numbers by whether order matters, find the one cell where a fact fits by its headers, and see two columns fill up for comparison. The leaflet fix step makes them diagnose three real layout slips among five parts, which is the editing skill the Year 6 writing composition statements ask for.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting options: whether a sub-heading should be the first sentence of a section, whether steps belong in bullets or a numbered list, and why a table helps (it compares one feature across all three animals versus it looks neater). The sorting, table and leaflet tasks then show the answer in action before the done message repeats it.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions on choosing devices, writing sub-headings and table headers, each wrong option tagged with its own message string through hint(), such as telling a learner who picks bullets for recipe steps that order matters so numbers fit. A correct streak is counted and a fresh question is drawn after each answer.

readability.evidence: The kid text is written for a Year 6 reader with short sentences and one idea each, and passes the learner readability target in the validator. The terms heading, sub-heading, bullet points, numbered list, table, column and header are each named and explained the first time, matching the vocabulary of the English National Curriculum appendix.

no_filler.evidence: No stock openers or padding: every paragraph either teaches a device, says when to use it, or names a slip. The examples are concrete wildlife guides about hedgehogs, bats and squirrels instead of generic text, and the content gate's filler checks passed with explanation similarity under the 12 percent limit.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on a 360 px Android viewport and iPhone 13 show sections, chips, the three-column table and the Do/Don't columns all fit, with long fact and tip cards wrapping inside their boxes. Chips and cells are at least 40 px tall, and every drag or swipe has a button twin so nothing needs precise dragging.

accessibility.evidence: axe runs clean in dark and light themes on desktop and iPhone 13 in the browser walkthrough. The canvas has an aria-label, each step offers buttons for every drag, tap or swipe, and feedback is announced through the shared status line, so the whole lab can be completed by keyboard or screen reader.

sources: DfE (2013) English programmes of study: key stage 2, Years 5 and 6 writing composition, and English Appendix 2 Year 6 layout devices
Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts W.4.2a and W.5.2a (formatting such as headings to aid comprehension)
British Hedgehog Preservation Society and Hedgehog Street: hedgehog diet, 13 cm fence holes, hibernation, no milk
Bat Conservation Trust: bat diet and hibernation; The Wildlife Trusts: grey squirrels stay active in winter
